Sino-French War.subject: Indian Languages

Sino-French War.fact: In the Battle of Fuzhou (also called the Battle of the Pagoda Anchorage) on 23 August 1884, the French took their revenge for the Bắc Lệ Ambush. Sino-French War.subject: Indian Languages

Sino-French War.fact: Patriotic indignation spread to British Hong Kong. In September 1884 dock workers in Hong Kong refused to repair the French ironclad La Galissonnière, which had suffered shell damage in the August naval engagements.

Sino-French War.subject: Indian Languages

Sino-French War.fact: Finally, on 3 February 1885, Brière de l'Isle began his advance from Chũ with a column of just under 7,200 troops, accompanied by 4,500 coolies. Spanish conquest of Petén.fact: This relationship did not hinder the Spanish from using the Qʼeqchiʼ to help conquer and reduce the Manche Chʼol. The Itza became fearful that the newly converted Manche Chʼol would lead the Spanish to Nojpetén.

Spanish conquest of Petén.subject: Indian Languages

Spanish conquest of Petén.fact: Between 1685 and 1689, the Qʼeqchiʼ of Cobán and Cahabón were forced to assist the Spanish in their armed expeditions against the Manche Chʼol and in forcibly relocating them to Verapaz.

Spanish conquest of Petén.subject: Indian Languages
Spanish conquest of Petén.question: The most important of these was Sakbʼajlan on the Lacantún River in eastern _____, now in Mexico, which was renamed as Nuestra Señora de Dolores, or Dolores del Lakandon, in April 1695
Spanish conquest of Petén.fact: The most important of these was Sakbʼajlan on the Lacantún River in eastern Chiapas, now in Mexico, which was renamed as Nuestra Señora de Dolores, or Dolores del Lakandon, in April 1695. This was one part of a three-pronged attack against the independent inhabitants of Petén and neighbouring Chiapas; a second group joined up with Barrios Leal having marched from Huehuetenango.

Spanish conquest of Petén.subject: Indian Languages
Spanish conquest of Petén.question: In the first half of the _____th century, Spain established neighbouring colonies in Yucatán to the north and Guatemala to the south
Spanish conquest of Petén.fact: In the first half of the 16th century, Spain set up neighbouring colonies in Yucatán to the north and Guatemala to the south. Spanish missionaries laid the groundwork for the extension of colonial administration in the extreme south of Petén from 1596 onwards, but no further Spanish entry of central Petén took place until 1618 and 1619 when missionaries arrived at the Itza capital, having travelled from the Spanish town of Mérida in Yucatán.

Spanish conquest of Petén.subject: Indian Languages
Spanish conquest of Petén.question: In 1628 the _____ʼol of the south were placed under the administration of the colonial governor of Verapaz within the Captaincy General of Guatemala
Spanish conquest of Petén.fact: In 1628 the Manche Chʼol of the south were placed under the administration of the colonial governor of Verapaz within the Captaincy General of Guatemala. The Manche Chʼol unsuccessfully rebelled against Spanish control in 1633.

Spanish conquest of Petén.subject: Indian Languages

Spanish conquest of Petén.subject: Indian Languages

Spanish conquest of Petén.fact: The extreme southeast of Petén experiences the largest variations in temperature and rainfall, with precipitation reaching as much as 3,000 millimetres (120 in) in a year.

Spanish conquest of Petén.fact: It is estimated that 88% of the inhabitants died during the first decade of colonial rule because of disease and war.

Spanish conquest of Petén.fact: In 1628 the towns of the Manche Chʼol were placed under the administration of the governor of Verapaz, with Dominican friar Francisco Morán as their ecclesiastical head. Morán favoured a more robust approach to the conversion of the Manche and moved Spanish soldiers into the region to protect against raids from the Itza to the north.

Spanish conquest of Petén.subject: Indian Languages
Spanish conquest of Petén.question: From 1692 to 1694, _____ friars Antonio Margil and Melchor López were active among the Manche and Lakandon Chʼol
Spanish conquest of Petén.fact: Towards the end of the 17th century Spanish priorities changed, and the failure of the peaceful efforts of the Dominicans to convert the Chʼol combined with the increasing British presence in the Caribbean led the colonial authorities to end the Dominican monopoly and allow the Franciscans and other orders to enter the region; military options were also viewed more favourably. From 1692 to 1694, Franciscan friars Antonio Margil and Melchor López were active among the Manche and Lakandon Chʼol.

Spanish conquest of Petén.subject: Indian Languages
Spanish conquest of Petén.question: After 1700 the _____ʼol ceased to play any part in the history of Petén
Spanish conquest of Petén.fact: After 1700 the Manche Chʼol ceased to play any part in the history of Petén. In 1692 the Council of the Indies ordered that the Manche Chʼol and the Mopan be dealt with decisively.

Spanish conquest of Petén.subject: Indian Languages

Spanish conquest of Petén.fact: The soldiers were sacrificed to the Maya gods, with their hearts cut from their chests and their heads impaled on stakes around the town. The fate of the leader of Delgado's Maya companions was no better.

Spanish conquest of Petén.fact: After the sacrifice of the Spanish soldiers, the Itza took Delgado, cut his heart out and dismembered him; they displayed his head on a stake with the others. The fate of the leader of Delgado's Maya companions was no better.

Spanish conquest of Petén.fact: With no word from Delgado's escort, Mirones sent two Spanish soldiers with Bernardino Ek, a Maya scout, to learn their fate. Ek escaped and returned to Mirones with the news.

Spanish conquest of Petén.subject: Indian Languages

Spanish conquest of Petén.fact: Soon afterwards, on 27 January 1624, an Itza war party led by AjKʼin Pʼol caught Mirones and his soldiers off guard and unarmed in the church at Sakalum and slaughtered them.

Spanish conquest of Petén.fact: A number of local Maya men and women had also been hanged but not decapitated, and the attackers had burned the town. The Maya governor of Oxkutzcab, Fernando Kamal, set out with 150 Maya archers to track the warleader down; they succeeded in capturing the Itza captain and his followers, together with silverware from the looted Sakalum church and items belonging to Mirones.

Spanish conquest of Petén.fact: The expedition proceeded northwards through Chʼol territory and into Mopan territory; there they camped at Mopan town (modern San Luis).

The Itzas at the lake handed over an open letter written by Avendaño before his departure from Nojpetén as a token of friendship between the Itza and the Spanish.

Spanish conquest of Petén.subject: Indian Languages
Spanish conquest of Petén.question: Friar Juan de _____ was enthused by the letter and wished to travel on to Nojpetén himself
Spanish conquest of Petén.fact: Friar Juan de San Buenaventura was enthused by the letter and wished to travel on to Nojpetén himself. He arrived at Lake Petén Itza with 60 musketeers, friar San Buenaventura and another Franciscan and allied Yucatec Maya warriors.

Spanish conquest of Petén.subject: Indian Languages
Spanish conquest of Petén.question: García sent captain Pedro de _____, his senior officer, on towards the lake
Spanish conquest of Petén.fact: García sent captain Pedro de Zubiaur, his senior officer, on towards the lake. On 2 February the expedition was approached by two Itza warriors who told them of a recent battle between a Guatemalan expedition and the Itza; these two Itzas guided the party to a nearby Itza settlement, and the letter from Avendaño was shown to captain Zubiaur, convincing him that he could advance safely.

Spanish conquest of Petén.subject: Indian Languages

Spanish conquest of Petén.fact: He arrived at Lake Petén Itza with 60 musketeers, friar San Buenaventura and another Franciscan and allied Yucatec Maya warriors.

Spanish conquest of Petén.subject: Indian Languages
Spanish conquest of Petén.question: The port town of Chʼichʼ was abandoned but a large number of canoes approached, judged to be as many as 300 by the Spanish captain, bearing perhaps 2,000 _____ warriors
Spanish conquest of Petén.fact: He arrived at Lake Petén Itza with 60 musketeers, friar San Buenaventura and another Franciscan and allied Yucatec Maya warriors. On 2 February the expedition was approached by two Itza warriors who told them of a recent battle between a Guatemalan expedition and the Itza; these two Itzas guided the party to a nearby Itza settlement, and the letter from Avendaño was shown to captain Zubiaur, convincing him that he could advance safely.

Spanish conquest of Petén.subject: Indian Languages

Spanish conquest of Petén.fact: At this point the Spanish soldiers opened fire with their muskets, and the Itza retreated across the lake with their prisoners. The Spanish party retreated from the lake shore and regrouped on open ground where they were surrounded by about 2,000 Itza warriors who attempted to disarm them; the Itzas managed to seize another Spaniard and immediately struck off his head.

Spanish conquest of Petén.subject: Indian Languages
Spanish conquest of Petén.question: At this point about 10,000 Itza archers appeared from canoes concealed among the lakeside mangroves, and _____ ordered his men to fire a volley that killed between 30 and 40 Itzas
Spanish conquest of Petén.fact: At this point about 10,000 Itza archers appeared from canoes concealed among the lakeside mangroves, and Zubiaur ordered his men to fire a volley that killed between 30 and 40 Itzas. A Christian Maya musketeer and six other Indians fled at the start of the battle and took news to García that the entire expedition had been slaughtered; Zubiaur and the survivors of his expedition marched back into the base camp at Chuntuki two days later.

Spanish conquest of Petén.subject: Indian Languages
Spanish conquest of Petén.question: Ursúa later reported that the Spanish prisoners were taken back to _____én where they were all killed; this was also confirmed by AjChan at a later date
Spanish conquest of Petén.fact: Ursúa later reported that the Spanish prisoners were taken back to Nojpetén where they were all killed; this was also confirmed by AjChan at a later date. The bones of the dead were said to have been found by the Spanish after the final assault on Nojpetén in 1697; AjKʼin Kan Ekʼ, the Itza high priest, later reported that he had bound San Buenaventura and his companion into cross shapes and cut out their hearts.

Spanish conquest of Petén.subject: Indian Languages
Spanish conquest of Petén.question: This turn of events convinced Martín de Ursúa that _____ʼ would not surrender peacefully, and he began to organise an all-out assault on Nojpetén
Spanish conquest of Petén.fact: The bones of the dead were said to have been found by the Spanish after the final assault on Nojpetén in 1697; AjKʼin Kan Ekʼ, the Itza high priest, later reported that he had bound San Buenaventura and his companion into cross shapes and cut out their hearts. Spanish conquest of Petén.fact: The enlistment of previously authorised reinforcements was now urgent, but was hindered when 70 of 100 soldiers mutinied and never reached García's camp.

Spanish conquest of Petén.fact: In the second half of 1695 President Barrios began planning another expedition against the Itza from Verapaz, following harsh criticism of Juan Díaz de Velasco's retreat from near Lake Petén Itzá in April of that year.

Spanish conquest of Petén.fact: Barrios died in November, and oidor José de Escals became acting head of the Guatemalan colonial administration.

Spanish conquest of Petén.fact: Amésqueta marched his men through torrential rain from Cahabón to Mopán, arriving on 25 February 1696; the Guatemalans were still unaware of the clashes between García's forces and the Itza.

Spanish conquest of Petén.fact: He was also accompanied by AjKʼixaw, the Itza nobleman who had been taken prisoner on Díaz's previous expedition, who served as a trusted guide, scout and translator.

Spanish conquest of Petén.fact: They set out from Mopán on 7 March and left some sick soldiers with some supplies after five days, they then caught up with an advance party of roadbuilders and their military escort at Río Chakal.

Spanish conquest of Petén.fact: He left Mopán on 10 March 1696 with friar Agustín Cano and about 10 soldiers.

Spanish conquest of Petén.fact: They followed Díaz's trail to the shore of Lake Petén Itzá near to the Itza capital. As they scouted along the south shore they were shadowed by about 30 Itza canoes, and more Itzas approached by land but kept a safe distance.

Spanish conquest of Petén.fact: The demoralised Spanish garrison at Chuntuki buried their weapons and ammunition and retreated five leagues (approximately 13 miles or 21 km) back towards Campeche.

Spanish conquest of Yucatán.subject: Indian Languages

Spanish conquest of Yucatán.fact: At Chaktumal, Montejo learnt that shipwrecked Spanish sailor Gonzalo Guerrero was in the region, and Montejo sent messages to him, inviting him to return to join his compatriots, but the Mayanised Guerrero declined. The Maya at Chaktumal fed false information to the Spanish, and Montejo was unable to find Ávila and link up with him.

Spanish conquest of Yucatán.subject: Indian Languages
Spanish conquest of Yucatán.question: Late in _____, Montejo left Ávila to oversee Xamanha and sailed north to loop around the Yucatán Peninsula and head for the Spanish colony of New Spain in central Mexico
Spanish conquest of Yucatán.fact: Late in 1528, Montejo left Ávila to oversee Xamanha and sailed north to loop around the Yucatán Peninsula and head for the Spanish colony of New Spain in central Mexico.

Spanish conquest of Yucatán.fact: Alonso d' Ávila was sent from eastern Yucatán to conquer Acalan, which extended southeast of the Laguna de Terminos. In 1530 Ávila set up Salamanca de Acalan as a base from which to launch new attempts to conquer Yucatán.

Spanish conquest of Yucatán.fact: Alonso d' Ávila was sent from eastern Yucatán to conquer Acalan, which extended southeast of the Laguna de Terminos. In 1530 Ávila set up Salamanca de Acalan as a base from which to launch new attempts to conquer Yucatán.

Spanish conquest of Yucatán.fact: In 1530 Ávila set up Salamanca de Acalan as a base from which to launch new attempts to conquer Yucatán. Ávila soon abandoned the new settlement and set off across the lands of the Kejache to Champotón, arriving there towards the end of 1530.

Spanish conquest of Yucatán.fact: Upon his release, he met up with his son in Xicalango, Tabasco, and they then both rejoined Ávila at Champotón.

Spanish conquest of Yucatán.fact: Alonso d' Ávila was sent overland to Chauaca in the east of the peninsula, passing through Maní, where he was well received by the Xiu Maya.

Spanish conquest of Yucatán.question: Ávila continued southeast to _____ where he founded the Spanish town of Villa Real ("Royal Town")
Spanish conquest of Yucatán.fact: Ávila continued southeast to Chetumal where he set up the Spanish town of Villa Real ("Royal Town").

Spanish conquest of Yucatán.fact: Ávila continued southeast to Chetumal where he set up the Spanish town of Villa Real ("Royal Town"). The local Maya fiercely resisted the placement of the new Spanish colony and Ávila and his men were forced to abandon Villa Real and make for Honduras in canoes.

Spanish conquest of Yucatán.subject: Indian Languages
Spanish conquest of Yucatán.question: At Campeche, the Maya amassed a strong force and attacked the city; the Spanish were able to fight them off, a battle in which the elder _____ was almost killed
Spanish conquest of Yucatán.fact: At Campeche, the Maya amassed a strong force and attacked the city; the Spanish were able to fight them off, a battle in which the elder Montejo was almost killed. After this battle, the younger Francisco de Montejo was despatched to the northern Cupul province, where the lord Naabon Cupul reluctantly allowed him to found the Spanish town of Ciudad Real at Chichén Itzá.

Spanish conquest of Yucatán.fact: The local Maya fiercely resisted the placement of the new Spanish colony and Ávila and his men were forced to abandon Villa Real and make for Honduras in canoes. Spanish conquest of Yucatán.fact: After this battle, the younger Francisco de Montejo was despatched to the northern Cupul province, where the lord Naabon Cupul reluctantly allowed him to found the Spanish town of Ciudad Real at Chichén Itzá. Spanish conquest of Yucatán.fact: In the spring of 1534 he rejoined his father in the Chakan province at Dzikabal, near Tʼho (the modern city of Mérida).

Spanish conquest of Yucatán.fact: In the spring of 1534 he rejoined his father in the Chakan province at Dzikabal, near Tʼho (the modern city of Mérida). The Montejos, after reuniting at Dzikabal, set up a new Spanish town at Dzilam, although the Spanish suffered hardships there.

Spanish conquest of Yucatán.subject: Indian Languages

Spanish conquest of Yucatán.fact: He was accompanied by the friendly Chel lord Namux Chel, who travelled on horseback, and two of the lord's cousins, who were taken in chains.

Spanish conquest of Yucatán.subject: Indian Languages
Spanish conquest of Yucatán.question: Towards the end of _____ or the beginning of the next year, Montejo the Elder and his son retreated from Campeche to Veracruz, taking their remaining soldiers with them
Spanish conquest of Yucatán.fact: Towards the end of 1534 or the beginning of the next year, Montejo the Elder and his son retreated from Campeche to Veracruz, taking their remaining soldiers with them.

Spanish conquest of Yucatán.fact: His initial efforts were proving successful when Captain Lorenzo de Godoy arrived in Champotón at the command of soldiers despatched there by Montejo the Younger.

Godoy and Testera were soon in conflict and the friar was forced to abandon Champotón and return to central Mexico.

Spanish conquest of Yucatán.fact: His initial efforts were proving successful when Captain Lorenzo de Godoy arrived in Champotón at the command of soldiers despatched there by Montejo the Younger. Spanish conquest of Yucatán.fact: Shortly after establishing the Spanish presence in Campeche, Montejo the Younger summoned the local Maya lords and commanded them to submit to the Spanish Crown.

Spanish conquest of Yucatán.fact: The lord of the Canul Maya refused to submit and Montejo the Younger sent his cousin against them; Montejo himself remained in Campeche awaiting reinforcements. Montejo the Younger's cousin met the Canul Maya at Chakan, not far from Tʼho.

Spanish conquest of Yucatán.subject: Indian Languages

Tikal.fact: The badly eroded Altar 21 at Caracol described how Tikal suffered this disastrous defeat in a major war in April 562. It seems that Caracol was an ally of Calakmul in the wider conflict between that city and Tikal, with the defeat of Tikal having a lasting impact upon the city.

Tikal.subject: Indian Languages
Tikal.question: Filmmaker George Lucas used Tikal as a filming location for the fictional moon Yavin _____ in the first Star Wars film, which premiered in 1977
Tikal.fact: In 1979, the Guatemalan government began a further archaeological project at Tikal, which continued through to 1984. Filmmaker George Lucas used Tikal as a filming location for the fictional moon Yavin 4 in the first Star Wars film, which premiered in 1977.

Tikal.question: A huge set of earthworks discovered by Dennis E. Puleston and Donald Callender in the 1960s rings Tikal with a 6-meter (_____) wide trench behind a rampart
Tikal.fact: A huge set of earthworks discovered by Dennis E. Puleston and Donald Callender in the 1960s rings Tikal with a 6-meter (20 ft) wide trench behind a rampart.

Tikal.subject: Indian Languages
Tikal.question: For example, the Maya widely adopted the dotleaf waterlily, _____ ampla, in their reservoirs' bodies of water
Tikal.fact: For example, the Maya widely adopted the dotleaf waterlily, Nymphaea ampla, in their reservoirs' bodies of water.

Tikal.question: the drinking water in the _____ reservoir was filtered through layers of Clinoptilolite and Mordenite zeolites, in addition to coarse to very coarse sand-sized quartz crystals
Tikal.fact: The Corriental reservoir at Tikal contained a novel water filtration system that removed harmful microbes and insoluble or soluble toxins. the drinking water in the Corriental reservoir was filtered through layers of Clinoptilolite and Mordenite zeolites, in addition to coarse to very coarse sand-sized quartz crystals.

Tikal.subject: Indian Languages
Tikal.question: In addition to physical filtration, geochemical analyses of sediment cores from the _____ and Palace reservoirs have revealed severe historical mercury contamination
Tikal.fact: In addition to physical filtration, geochemical analyses of sediment cores from the Temple and Palace reservoirs have revealed severe historical mercury contamination.

Tikal.question: This toxicity resulted primarily from the widespread ceremonial application of cinnabar-based pigments on monumental architecture and stelae throughout the _____
Tikal.fact: This toxicity resulted primarily from the widespread ceremonial application of cinnabar-based pigments on monumental architecture and stelae throughout the Classic Period.

Tikal.fact: Hence, water and by extension, reservoirs became a significant part of the Maya power structure. This also means that a way for Maya rulers to concentrate their power would be through proper water management.

Tikal.fact: 804 and 938 show a 36% to 56% drop in precipitation.

Tikal.fact: On the north side it is bordered by the North Acropolis and on the south by the Central Acropolis. Tikal.fact: The Central Acropolis is a palace complex just south of the Great Plaza. The North Acropolis, together with the Great Plaza immediately to the south, is one of the most studied architectural groups in the Maya area; the Tikal Project excavated a massive trench across the complex, thoroughly investigating its construction history.

Tikal.fact: It is a complex group with construction beginning in the Preclassic Period, around 350 BC.

Tikal.fact: It is a complex group with construction beginning in the Preclassic Period, around 350 BC. It developed into a funerary complex for the ruling dynasty of the Classic Period, with each additional royal burial adding new temples on top of the older structures.

Tikal.subject: Indian Languages
Tikal.question: After AD 400 a row of tall pyramids was added to the earlier Northern Platform, which measured 100 by _____ (330 by 260 ft), gradually hiding it from view
Tikal.fact: After AD 400 a row of tall pyramids was added to the earlier Northern Platform, which measured 100 by 80 meters (330 by 260 ft), gradually hiding it from view.

Tikal.subject: Indian Languages
Tikal.question: By the 9th century AD, 43 stelae and 30 altars had been erected in the _____; 18 of these monuments were carved with hieroglyphic texts and royal portraits
Tikal.fact: By the 9th century AD, 43 stelae and 30 altars had been erected in the North Acropolis; 18 of these monuments were carved with hieroglyphic texts and royal portraits. The North Acropolis continued to receive burials into the Postclassic Period.

Tikal.subject: Indian Languages
Tikal.question: The North Acropolis continued to receive burials into the _____
Tikal.fact: The North Acropolis continued to receive burials into the Postclassic Period.

Tikal.subject: Indian Languages
Tikal.question: The South Acropolis is found next to _____ was built upon a large basal platform that covers an area of more than 20,000 square meters (220,000 sq ft)
Tikal.fact: The South Acropolis is found next to Temple V. It was built upon a large basal platform that covers an area of more than 20,000 square meters (220,000 sq ft).

Tikal.subject: Indian Languages
Tikal.question: The Plaza of the _____ is to the west of the South Acropolis
Tikal.fact: The Plaza of the Seven Temples is to the west of the South Acropolis. The Mundo Perdido is to the west of the Plaza of the Seven Temples.

Tikal.subject: Indian Languages
Tikal.question: The Mundo Perdido is to the west of the Plaza of the _____
Tikal.fact: The Plaza of the Seven Temples is to the west of the South Acropolis. The Mundo Perdido is to the west of the Plaza of the Seven Temples.

Tikal.subject: Indian Languages

Tikal.fact: By AD 250–300 its architectural style was influenced by the great metropolis of Teotihuacan in the Valley of Mexico, including the use of the talud-tablero form.

Tikal.subject: Indian Languages
Tikal.question: 250–600) the _____ became one of the twin foci of the city, the other being the North Acropolis
Tikal.fact: The Mundo Perdido complex was rebuilt many times over the course of its history. 250–600) the Mundo Perdido became one of the twin foci of the city, the other being the North Acropolis.

Tikal.subject: Indian Languages
Tikal.question: The Mundo Perdido complex was given its name by the archaeologists of the University of Pennsylvania; it is centered upon the _____ and a small platform to the west of it
Tikal.fact: The Mundo Perdido is to the west of the Plaza of the Seven Temples. It is the largest ceremonial complex dating from the Preclassic period at Tikal.

Tikal.subject: Indian Languages
Tikal.question: To the south of Mundo Perdido, recent _____ excavations have revealed a one-third size replication of La Ciudadela, or The Citadel, in Teotihuacan
Tikal.fact: To the south of Mundo Perdido, recent 2021 excavations have revealed a one-third size replication of La Ciudadela, or The Citadel, in Teotihuacan.

Tikal.fact: Group G lies just south of the Mendez Causeway.

Tikal.fact: Group H is centered on a large plaza to the north of the Great Plaza.

Tikal.question: It is bordered by temples dating to the _____
Tikal.fact: It is bordered by temples dating to the Late Classic.

Tikal.subject: Indian Languages
Tikal.question: The entire complex was built at once and these complexes were built at 20-year (or k'atun) intervals during the _____
Tikal.fact: The entire complex was built at once and these complexes were built at 20-year (or k'atun) intervals during the Late Classic. It was once thought that these complexes were unique to Tikal but rare examples have now been found at other sites, such as Yaxha and Ixlu, and they may reflect the extent of Tikal's political dominance in the Late Classic.

Tikal.subject: Indian Languages
Tikal.question: The first twin-pyramid complex was built in the early _____th century in the East Plaza
Tikal.fact: The first twin-pyramid complex was built in the early 6th century in the East Plaza.

Tikal.fact: It was built by Yax Nuun Ayiin II in 771 in order to mark the end of the 17th K'atun.

Tikal.subject: Indian Languages
Tikal.question: The most prominent surviving buildings include six very large pyramids, labelled _____ I – VI, each of which support a temple structure on their summits
Tikal.fact: The most prominent surviving buildings include six very large pyramids, labelled Temples I – VI, each of which support a temple structure on their summits. It is estimated that each of these major temples could have been built in as little as two years.

Tikal.fact: Some of these pyramids are over 60 meters (200 feet) high.

Tikal.fact: The temple rises 47 meters (154 ft) high.

Tikal.fact: The tomb of the king was discovered by Aubrey Trik of the University of Pennsylvania in 1962.

Tikal.subject: Indian Languages
Tikal.question: The outermost lintel is plain but the two inner lintels were carved, some of the beams were removed in the 19th century and their location is unknown, while others were taken to museums in _____
Tikal.fact: The outermost lintel is plain but the two inner lintels were carved, some of the beams were removed in the 19th century and their location is unknown, while others were taken to museums in Europe.

Tikal.subject: Indian Languages

Tikal.fact: Temple II (also called the Temple of the Mask) it was built around AD 700 and stands 38 meters (125 ft) high.

Tikal.fact: The temple was dedicated to the wife of Jasaw Chan Kʼawil, although no tomb was found.

Tikal.fact: One of the beams from this lintel is now in the American Museum of Natural History in New York City.

Tikal.fact: It stood 55 meters (180 ft) tall and contained an elaborately sculpted but damaged roof lintel, possibly showing Dark Sun engaged in a ritual dance around AD 810.

Tikal.subject: Indian Languages

Tikal.fact: Temple IV is the tallest temple-pyramid at Tikal, measuring 70 meters (230 ft) from the plaza floor level to the top of its roof comb.

Tikal.fact: Temple V stands south of the Central Acropolis and is the mortuary pyramid of an as yet unidentified ruler.

Tikal.fact: Temple 33 was a funerary pyramid erected over the tomb of Siyaj Chan Kʼawiil I (known as Burial 48) in the North Acropolis.

Tikal.fact: It started life in the Early Classic as a wide basal platform decorated with large stucco masks that flanked the stairway. Later in the Early Classic a new superstructure was added, with its own masks and decorated panels.

Tikal.fact: It is built into the end of the East Plaza Ballcourt and possessed four entry doorways and three stairways, the fourth (south) side was too close to the Central Acropolis for a stairway on that side.

Tikal.fact: These are the most elaborately carved wooden lintels to have survived anywhere in the Maya region.
